title: Chevrolet’s Blazer Xtreme Hasn’t Lost Any of Its Intensity

body_markdown:
Compact trucks and their SUV-bodied brethren have occupied a small section of car culture since their inception over 40 years ago. The formula is simple: start with body-on-frame construction, add durable engines and transmissions, and include rugged suspensions.


But what made this genre take off were the options to perk up the interior and exterior, turning a basic work vehicle into an affordable street sensation. While many have played in this space, perhaps nobody did it with the success of Chevrolet’s S-10 truck and Blazer SUV when ordered with the Xtreme option package.


Hagerty Marketplace | Craig Zimmerman


Hagerty Marketplace | Craig Zimmerman


Hagerty Marketplace | Craig Zimmerman


What’s presented here might be the zenith of its genre. It was a factory-prepared street machine with the trappings of an aftermarket custom, but with a full warranty for stress-free operation. Its Vortec V6 engine cranked out a respectable 190 horsepower, and its Z87 suspension was lowered and stiffened with re-tuned dampers. The body eschews bare plastic trim for body-color paint, with deeply dished 16-inch alloy wheels, and a full body kit to visually lower the vehicle.


This is the Blazer Xtreme, perhaps the sportiest Blazer ever produced by Chevrolet. That statement may merit a rebuke in the comments, as Chevrolet made a TrailBlazer SS (2006-2009) with superior performance and a similar stance. But thanks to its two-door configuration, there’s a purity to the Blazer Xtreme that gives it a certain style that cannot be replicated in the era of four-door SUVs that replaced it.


Hagerty Marketplace | Craig Zimmerman


Hagerty Marketplace | Craig Zimmerman


Hagerty Marketplace | Craig Zimmerman


This particular Blazer Xtreme is a 2002 model, and it still possesses its OEM-tuned suspension, body kit, and unique wheels. It’s currently being auctioned on the[Hagerty Marketplace](https://www.hagerty.com/marketplace/auction/2002-Chevrolet-Blazer/c58508db-db64-4cd2-99cd-a3004030a552) , with 7 days to go and a high bid of $4000. There are a handful of imperfections after 126,000 miles of use, but what makes this Xtreme so intense is clear for everyone to see.


The stance is correct, the engine looks stock, and nobody cut up the interior to add an aftermarket stereo system. While Xtremes could be optioned with an “Accent Appearance Package” that added gold stripes, gold badges, and gold-painted wheel inserts, this example sits proud with a monochrome black body treatment.


Hagerty Marketplace | Craig Zimmerman


Hagerty Marketplace | Craig Zimmerman


Blazers of this era were often a foundation for show and sound, but this one remains true to the factory’s mission. Aside from a missing hubcap emblem, signs of dry rot on some tires, and a set of non-standard lights, this driver-quality Blazer Xtreme is prime for a time-machine trip down mini-trucking memory lane.


While nostalgia plays a significant role in this lowered Blazer’s modern existence, there’s no doubt that the soaring costs of modern trucks make a sporty two-door SUV appealing to a wider audience. Then and now, the Blazer Xtreme provided an admirable amount of bang for the buck.
